theme: Ten miracles, the King demonstrates the Kingdom’s arrival
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 8:1-9:38. Matthew gathers ten miracles into two chapters: a leper, a centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, a storm, two demon-possessed men, a paralytic, a dead girl, a woman with bleeding, two blind men, and a mute man. Read for what the miracles reveal about the King.
settingTheScene: After the Sermon on the Mount, in which Jesus spoke with authority, Matthew shows Jesus acting with authority. The Sermon was the King’s words, and these chapters are the King’s works. Each miracle demonstrates that the kingdom of heaven has arrived, and each shows power over a different enemy: disease, nature, demons, sin, and death. Alongside the miracles, Matthew places the cost of following him.
observation: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean” (8:2).
“Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith” (8:10).
“This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: He took our illnesses and bore our diseases” (8:17).
“Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (8:20).
“What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” (8:27).
“Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven” (9:2).
“I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (9:13).
“When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (9:36).
interpretation:
The first miracle is a leper, the most unclean person in Israel. The law said that a leper must keep away and cry “Unclean!” Yet Jesus touches him, and instead of Jesus becoming unclean, the man becomes clean. Then comes a Roman centurion, a Gentile, who recognizes that Jesus needs only to say the word. Jesus is amazed at his faith and says that many will come from east and west to sit at table with Abraham. The kingdom is wider than Israel.

On the Sea of Galilee, a storm threatens to sink the boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind and the waves, and there is a great calm. The disciples ask, “What sort of man is this?” Only God commands the sea (Psalm 107:29). He then sends demons into pigs and heals a paralyzed man. Here the order is striking: he first says “Your sins are forgiven,” and only then heals the body. The scribes call it blasphemy, and they are right that only God can forgive sins. Jesus proves his authority by healing.

Matthew himself, the tax collector, is called to follow. Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners and says he is a physician for the sick. Then a ruler’s daughter is raised, a woman’s bleeding is healed, the blind see, and the mute speak. 

The section ends with Jesus’ compassion. He sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd and says the harvest is plentiful but the laborers are few. The miracles are not displays. They show the heart of the Messiah, who has come to rescue and to gather.
connection: Leviticus 13 and 14 describe the laws for leprosy. Psalm 107:23-30 describes God calming the storm. Isaiah 53:4 is quoted in 8:17. Mark 2:1-12 gives a fuller account of the paralytic. Hosea 6:6 is quoted in 9:13. Ezekiel 34:5 describes shepherdless sheep. John 11:25: “I am the resurrection and the life.” Hebrews 4:15: we have a high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses.
application:
Pray the leper’s prayer: “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” Name the specific thing you need cleansed or healed.

When storms come, remember that Jesus is in the boat. Say aloud, “Even the winds and sea obey him.”

Ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers, and ask whether you may be one.
prayerPrompts: Tell Jesus you believe, and ask him to help your unbelief.
Ask him to make you clean where you need cleansing.
Thank him for his power over storms, sin, and death.
